s: practices cruelty of masters toward slaves [toward female servants and other slaves] Megallis, the wife of Damophilus, was as cruel as he was toward maidservants and other slaves under her control. Her abuse contributed to the slaves' decision to rise up.

l: Cleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cleon, a Cilician and Sicilian near Mount Taurus, had practiced robbery since boyhood. Inspired by Eunus's success, he led neighboring slaves in revolt, plundered Agrigentum, joined Eunus as general of five thousand, fought Romans, and was killed in a sortie from Enna; his body was exposed.

l: Roman generals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: fight servile war in Sicily [against the rebel slaves] Roman generals repeatedly fought the Sicilian rebels and were often defeated because of the rebels' superior numbers. Rupilius eventually recovered Taurominium, captured Enna, defeated the remaining rebels, and cleared Sicily of thieves and robbers.

l: Rupilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: clears Sicily [of thieves and robbers] Rupilius commanded the Roman campaign against the Sicilian slave revolt. He recovered Taurominium after a prolonged siege, captured Comaon, killed Cleon during a sortie from Enna, took Enna by betrayal, and later cleared Sicily of the remaining rebels.

l: Cimbrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Cimbrians ravaged and harassed Gaul and inflicted many losses on the Romans. Rome had lost sixty thousand men in the war against them while also facing the Sicilian slave rebellion.

l: Caius Marius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Caius Marius, also called Gaius Marius, was a Roman commander whose rise began after being slighted as an ambassador and said to have been a publican. He diligently pursued military affairs, became an expert and famous soldier, and won the Roman army’s love through generosity and affability. His command brought repeated Roman victories; with Bocchus’s help he trapped Jugurtha and had him delivered to Lucius Sylla, and he defeated both Jugurtha and Bocchus in great battles. Renowned when young for ambition, courage, lack of covetousness, and achievements in Europe and Africa, he later sought Mithridates’ wealth and Sylla’s province, contributing to civil war and destruction in Italy. After opposing Caesar, fighting and losing to Sylla, and fleeing to Praeneste, he ended his life through a faithful servant when escape was impossible.

l: Bocchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Bocchus, African king of Libya, rejects war with Rome, seeks pardon and alliance through Marius, and helps seize Jugurtha to secure safety and avoid Roman punishment.

l: Jugurtha, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Jugurtha is an African king and king of Numidia, brother of Adherbal and father-in-law of Bocchus. After routing the Numidians, he besieges Adherbal at Cirta, ignores Roman orders, starves the city into surrender, kills Adherbal and Italians who aided him. Later Marius summons him deceptively; he is seized and delivered bound to Lucius Sylla.

l: Lucius Licinius Lucullus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lucius Licinius Lucullus, a Roman general, was appointed to suppress Sicilian rebels. After raising troops in Rome and Capua, he entered Sicily, defeated Tryphon and Athenion near Scirthsea, and pursued fugitives to Tricala. His failure to take it led to judgment and banishment for neglecting duty.

l: fugitive slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_defeated_by Lucius Licinius Lucullus [through the betrayal of Apollonius] The fugitive slaves first gained strength through revolts across Sicily, often killing their masters and seizing strongholds. They defeated Roman forces, captured arms and prisoners, expanded into an army of tens of thousands, established kings, occupied territory, and fought Rome for almost four years before being defeated.

l: Roman army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Roman army fought repeatedly against the rebel slaves in Sicily. Roman forces sometimes suffered defeats, including the loss of arms at the battle near Mount Cyprianus and the defeat near Morgantium, but later campaigns under Lucullus and Caius Aquilius broke the rebellion.

l: Licinius Nerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Licinius Nerva, a Roman praetor or proconsul in Sicily, first frees more than eight hundred enslaved people under a decree, then reverses course under local pressure, returns petitioners to masters, helps provoke a slave conspiracy, and unsuccessfully commands forces against it.

l: Salvius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Salvius, a fortune-teller chosen king by rebellious fugitive slaves, was also called Tryphon. As rebel king he organized and enlarged their army through raids, divided it into three bodies, besieged Morgantium, defeated a Roman army nearby, and proclaimed liberty to its slaves.

l: Athenion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Athenion, a Cilician slave and skilled astrologer, became leader and king of a rebel force around Aegesta and Lilybaeum. He commanded three thousand men, cooperated with Tryphon, was seized and released, wounded Romans near Scirthsea, fled wounded, and was killed by Caius Aquilius.

l: Tryphon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tryphon, formerly Salvius, became king of rebel slaves, strengthened Tricala as his capital, summoned then seized Athenion, led rebels against Lucullus, fled after defeat near Scirthsea, and died.

l: Tricala, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tricala is Tryphon’s royal seat, a strongly fortified high rock with springs, vineyards, olive plantations, and rich land. Tryphon strengthened it, built institutions, and centered rebellion there; Roman forces besieged it but withdrew after losses.

l: Caius Aquilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Roman general appointed against rebels after becoming consul with Caius Marius; he defeated and killed Athenion in single combat despite a head wound, then pursued surviving rebels until resistance collapsed.

l: Quintus Pompoedius Silo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Quintus Pompoedius Silo was a Marsian of high standing, a Marsian general, and an Italian consul. He led the Marsi and commanded northern and western Italy, later leading remaining Italians from Aesernia. He marched toward Rome with armed supporters to seek freedom, but Caius Domitius persuaded him to return and petition the Senate. In battle against Romans, he killed opponents but lost more than six thousand men.

l: Caius Apootua Motulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a consul [of the Italian government] Caius Apootua Motulus was chosen as the other Italian consul because of his notable actions. He commanded the southern and eastern division of Italy. At about the same time, he took the city of Venusia in Apulia and carried away more than three thousand prisoners.

l: Cneius Pompeius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cneius Pompeius was a Roman consul, general, military commander, and praetor in Sicily. Hardened by austere discipline, he studied military affairs, trained an army, defeated Junius Brutus, and gained recognition. As consul during the Marsian war, he and Sylla repeatedly routed the Italians; in Sicily he administered justice diligently and was admired for gravity and sobriety.

l: Lucius Sylla, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lucius Sylla was a Roman consul, military leader, and later dictator. He gained fame through brave actions, helped Cneius Pompeius defeat the Italians, compelled neighboring territories and cities to obey Rome, and financed war by robbing temples. He opposed and defeated Marius in civil war, fought Mithridates in Asia, and gained control of Rome’s political affairs.

l: Caius Julius Caesar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Caius Julius Caesar, a Roman ruler surnamed Divus, is praised for humanity, clemency, moderation, eloquence, military skill, birth, and contempt for riches. Moved by Corinth's ruins, he sought to rebuild it. He opposed Gaius Marius, later fought Pompey amid internal slaughter, and ultimately gained unbounded power after consular authority was restricted.

l: Octavius Augustus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: gains empire [after defeating Antony] Octavius Augustus helped conduct the war against Brutus and Cassius after Caesar's murder. He later fought Antonius for supreme power, prevailed, and held the empire throughout his life.

l: Pompey, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pompey, called the Great for eminent services to the Romans under Sylla and through his own valor, besieges and destroys Lagnetia after conflict involving the Numantians. His conflict with Julius Caesar brings another civil war; after losing his army in a great battle, he is murdered near Alexandria.

l: Junius Brutus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Brutus was identified as one of Caesar's murderers. He fought the civil war conducted against him and Cassius by Lepidus, Antonius, and Octavius Augustus, and he died when that war ended.

l: Cassius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cassius was identified as one of Caesar's murderers. He fought alongside Brutus against Lepidus, Antonius, and Octavius Augustus, and he died when that civil war was concluded.

l: civil wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: include war against Brutus and Cassius [after Caesar's murder] The unit describes several civil wars involving Marius and Sylla, Julius Caesar and Pompey, Brutus and Cassius against Antonius and Augustus, and Augustus against Antonius. These conflicts caused extensive slaughter and repeatedly changed who controlled Rome.

l: sedition in Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sedition in Rome arose first from competition among Roman nobles for command of the war against Mithridates. A second great sedition was stirred up by Sylla and Marius, causing many thousands to perish. The account also connects later internal conflicts with the struggles between Caesar and Pompey and between Augustus and Antonius.

l: war against Mithridates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes sedition in Rome [through rivalry over its command] The war against Mithridates became the object of intense competition among Roman nobles because of the rewards and riches expected from it. Caius Julius Caesar and Gaius Marius disputed its command, while Sylla eventually led Roman forces in Asia against Mithridates.

l: war against the Jews, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The war against the Jews is introduced as the subject that follows the account of Roman civil conflicts. Before discussing it, the text says that the origin, laws, and customs of the Jewish nation should be explained.

l: Judea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Judea is described as the formerly deserted and uninhabited country where most of the expelled people settled. Moses led the colony there, established its institutions, and distributed its territories among the people.

l: Lucius Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lucius Tarquinius is Rome's wise, liberally educated, generous king and the father of Sextus Tarquinius.

l: virtue, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Virtue is a set of honorable qualities, including courage, prudence, justice, piety, wisdom, gentleness, sobriety, constancy, patience, frugality, loyalty, purity, affability, and generosity. It brings honor, esteem, lasting reputation, and renown, as shown by Lycurgus, Solon, Cyrus, and Publius Scipio. Learning and disciplined conduct cultivate it; neglect leads to luxury, tyranny, cruelty, and loss of power.

l: impiety and contempt of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Impiety and contempt of the gods are shown in figures such as Epopeus, Salmoneus, and Romulus Sylvius, who challenged, dishonored, or mocked the gods. Their conduct is presented as bringing destruction or divine punishment: Epopeus destroyed temples and altars, Salmoneus rejected sacrifices and imitated Jupiter's thunder, and Romulus Sylvius was struck dead by a thunderbolt.

l: laws and good government, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The unit presents laws and good government as foundations of strength, order, and public welfare. The Lacedaemonians became powerful while observing Lycurgus's laws but declined after neglecting them; Solon gained the Athenians toward virtue through laws and discipline; and Pittacus is praised as a prudent lawmaker who freed his country from tyranny, sedition, and war.

l: Pythagoreans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: avoid oaths [as much as possible] The Pythagoreans supported members of their society who fell into poverty, even when they had never met them, and sometimes risked their lives for one another. They practiced memory exercises, abstinence, moderation, and moral purity, and were highly esteemed by the Crotonians.

l: Damon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Damon, a Pythagorean and pupil of Phintias, agreed without hesitation to become hostage and die in Phintias's place. He remained prepared for execution until Phintias returned at the last moment.

l: Lysis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lysis, a Pythagorean, goes to Thebes, tutors Epaminondas in virtue, and adopts him as his son because of his excellent qualities.

l: Hipparchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hipparchus, brother of Thessalus and Hippias, ruled the Athenians tyrannically. His love for a beautiful boy placed him in peril and contributed to the conspiracy formed by Harmodius and Aristogiton.
